topic: Why indexing isn't just 'put an index on every foreign key' - the real cost of indexes in PostgreSQL
hook: Adding an index to every foreign key is one of the fastest ways to degrade PostgreSQL write throughput in production.
postText:
Adding an index to every foreign key is one of the fastest ways to degrade PostgreSQL write throughput in production.

Under heavy traffic, unmeasured indexes aren't free optimizations. They are a continuous tax on your database.

Here is what actually happens under the hood when you blindly index:

1. Write Amplification & Broken HOT Updates
Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE forces Postgres to write to every index page. Updating a row with 8 indexes creates 8 additional index writes, disabling Heap-Only Tuple (HOT) optimizations.

2. Shared Buffer Contamination
Indexes need memory to stay fast. Unused B-tree pages hog space in shared_buffers, constantly evicting actual warm cache data required by active queries.

3. Autovacuum Pressure & IOPS Bloat
More indexes mean slower autovacuum runs. Bloated index trees cause random I/O spikes, degrading disk performance over time.

Indexes should strictly serve actual query patterns analyzed via EXPLAIN ANALYZE, not defensive assumptions.

A missing index causes one slow query. Five unnecessary indexes degrade every single write across your entire table.

hook: Most junior developers think Redis is just for caching.
postText:
Most junior developers think Redis is just for caching.

Here is how experienced backend engineers actually leverage it:

1. Distributed Locks (Redlock)
Preventing two background workers from charging the same credit card or modifying inventory simultaneously.

2. Sliding Window Rate Limiting
Protecting critical endpoints using atomic ZADD and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE.

3. Ephemeral Idempotency Keys
Storing deduplication tokens with a 120-second TTL to safely ignore duplicate network retries.

4. Pub/Sub & Lightweight Task Buffers
Handling high-throughput messaging before needing the operational overhead of Kafka.

Caching key-value pairs is merely 10% of Redis's power.
The real superpower is atomic, in-memory concurrency primitives.

Writing clean, atomic primitives will always scale better than throwing hardware at concurrency bugs.

#backend #systemdesign #softwareengineering
